lesson_core_move: Determine whether a continuous-time signal is periodic by verifying that some positive time shift T satisfies x(t+T)=x(t) for every t, connecting the result to later period, angular frequency, and harmonic analysis.

images.lesson_core_move: Determine whether a continuous-time signal is periodic by verifying that some positive time shift T satisfies x(t+T)=x(t) for every t, connecting the result to later period, angular frequency, and harmonic analysis.
images.image_description: A clean continuous-time line plot on labeled time and amplitude axes showing a non-sinusoidal waveform that repeats exactly after a horizontal shift of 3 units. Show two identical cycles, with the first cycle spanning $0 \le t < 3$ and the second cycle spanning $3 \le t < 6$. Make matching landmarks easy to compare by including the same peak and trough pattern in both cycles. Include a visible horizontal bracket or arrow spanning one cycle length, but leave it unlabeled.

Make matching landmarks easy to compare by including the same peak and trough pattern in both cycles. Include a visible horizontal bracket or arrow spanning one cycle length, but leave it unlabeled.

outline_section.learning_goal: Read a plotted continuous-time signal, detect whether the pattern repeats after a positive shift, and name one visible shift that lines up adjacent cycles.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is an example.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not applicable; this section is an example.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean continuous-time line plot showing a waveform that repeats exactly after a positive shift, with at least two matching cycles visible on labeled time and amplitude axes.
visual_elements: visible period bracket or shift arrow
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a simple uncluttered graph with clear repeated structure. The same waveform segment should appear at least twice so the later practice questions can vary the displayed graph while keeping the same periodicity check.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices; one correct classification of the graph and one valid positive shift.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a graph of $x(t)$, decide whether the signal is periodic and select one positive shift that aligns one visible cycle with the next.
distractor_plan: Use one shift that matches a local feature but not the whole waveform.
Use one choice that halves or doubles the visible repeat interval.
Use one choice that says the signal is not periodic when the graph clearly repeats.
Use one choice that names a shift that lines up only part of the displayed cycle.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: From the graph of $x(t)$, decide whether the waveform repeats after a positive shift and identify one visible shift that works.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to compare matching landmarks on adjacent cycles and read the horizontal distance as a valid period.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The periodicity check now comes from a graph instead of a symbolic definition, but the logic is still the same: compare one copy of the waveform to the next.
solution_step_plan: Locate a clear landmark on the plotted waveform.
Find the same landmark on the next repeated copy.
Read the time difference as a candidate positive shift.
Check that the full waveform shape matches after that shift.
Conclude that the signal is periodic and state the shift.
practice_variation_axes: change the waveform shape while preserving the repeat structure
change the time scale of the graph
change the phase origin of the first visible cycle
vary whether the graph has a vertical offset without changing periodicity

outline_section.handoff_notes: The image should carry the repetition signal. Keep the graph clean and obvious, and do not drift into smallest-period or angular-frequency work.

prompt_blocks.text: Which option correctly classifies the signal and gives one positive shift that aligns one visible cycle with the next?

choice_blocks.text: The signal is periodic, and one valid positive shift is $T=3$.
The signal is periodic, and one valid positive shift is $T=1.5$.
The signal is periodic, and one valid positive shift is $T=6$.
The signal is periodic, and one valid positive shift is $T=2$.

question.correct_answer: The signal is periodic, and one valid positive shift is $T=3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph shows the same shape again after $3$ units, so matching landmarks line up from one cycle to the next.
Therefore the signal is periodic, and $T=3$ is one visible positive shift.

images.image_description: A clean continuous-time line plot on labeled time and amplitude axes showing a non-sinusoidal waveform that repeats exactly after a horizontal shift of 5 units. Shift the whole graph upward so the waveform sits above the horizontal axis, and make the first visible cycle begin at $t=1$ and the next at $t=6$. Show two identical cycles with matching peaks and troughs, and include a visible horizontal bracket or arrow spanning one cycle length, but leave it unlabeled.
